screens.title: What is Resource Exhaustion?
screens.narratorSegment: Resource exhaustion means one of the system's primary resources — C P U, memory, or disk input and output — is saturated and cannot meet demand. Symptoms often include sluggish interactive response, long application latencies, or processes stalling and crashing. The critical teaching point is that different resources create different signatures: C P U exhaustion increases user or system C P U percentages, but disk input and output problems frequently show up as high C P U wait time, meaning the C P U is idle while waiting for input and output. Memory exhaustion leads to heavy swapping, where pages are moved to disk and performance collapses. Correct identification matters because the remediation differs: killing a C P U-bound process frees C P U cycles, but killing a process that is causing heavy disk input and output might not immediately reduce wait time if the device remains saturated. A practical misconception to avoid is treating a high overall C P U usage number as a single cause; you must inspect detailed counters such as wa, si, and so. A quick example: if interactive shell prompts lag while top shows high wa and iostat shows %util near 100%, adding C P U cores will not fix the problem — faster storage or reducing input and output load will. Takeaway: look for the signature, not just the headline metric.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › What is Resource Exhaustion?
Resource Exhaustion — definition and symptoms
Recognize the distinct signatures of CPU, memory, and I/O pressure.
Core definition
A resource is exhausted when demand exceeds capacity and the system cannot supply work at required speed.
Common signatures
  • CPU: sustained high user/system percentages and runnable queue growth.
  • Memory: high swap activity, low available memory counters.
  • Disk I/O: high CPU wait (wa) and device %util near 100%.
Concrete example
A web server becomes slow. top shows 70% us and 20% wa. iostat shows /dev/sda %util 98 and await high. This points to disk I/O as the primary bottleneck, not CPU capacity.
Misconception
Don't assume high CPU total equals CPU-bound work; check wa and per-process metrics before acting.
Key Takeaway

Match observable metric signatures to the resource type before choosing a remediation path — that avoids wasted effort and incorrect fixes.

Try this
When diagnosing, capture both live output and a short iostat snapshot to distinguish CPU vs I/O causes.

screens.title: Live monitoring with top and htop
screens.narratorSegment: top and htop are your first-stop tools when a system feels slow. top gives a compact summary: load averages, C P U states, memory use, and a process list. Important fields to interpret include us (user C P U), sy (system C P U), and wa (input and output wait). High us suggests compute-bound processes, high sy points to kernel activity, and high wa indicates the C P U is waiting on input and output. htop offers the same data in a more readable, colorized form and simplifies actions such as sorting by memory or C P U and sending signals to processes. A common workflow: sort by C P U and note the top consumers, then switch sorting by memory to find processes holding large resident sets. Watch the run queue length too — a growing runnable queue combined with high us suggests adding C P U capacity or tuning parallelism. A typical mistake is focusing solely on the top process without checking overall C P U wait and device metrics. For example, if a process shows high C P U but wa is also high, some of the apparent C P U time may be caused by blocking input and output or kernel work. Practice: run top while inducing a C P U load generator and observe how us rises sharply; then induce disk input and output and see wa increase while the top process may still appear active. This practice helps you translate numbers into root causes.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › top & htop
Live monitor: top (compact)
Quick snapshot of system and processes; default sorts by CPU.
top - 12:34:56 up 10 days,  2:22,  1 user,  load average: 1.23, 0.98, 0.75
Tasks: 123 total,   2 running, 121 sleeping
%Cpu(s): 70.0 us, 10.0 sy, 18.0 wa,  0.0 id
Mem:  16G total, 14G used, 2G free,  1G buffers
  PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU %MEM COMMAND

  • Watch the CPU line for us, sy, wa to map behavior to causes.

Interactive: htop (user-friendly)
Color bars, easy sorting, and actions like killing or renicing processes.

Use htop to toggle tree view, sort by memory, and spot processes with large RES values. Remember: a process with high CPU and associated high wa suggests I/O wait; investigate the device with iostat next.

Common mistake
Killing the first seen process without confirming its role can stop critical system services.
Pro tip
Use a second terminal to run iostat while you watch wa in top to correlate CPU wait with device utilization.

screens.title: Memory signals: free, vmstat, and swapping
screens.narratorSegment: Memory exhaustion shows up as low available memory and active swapping. The free command with human-readable flags gives a quick snapshot of total and available memory, as well as swap size and use. Pay attention to the line labeled -/+ buffers/cache which better reflects memory available to applications because kernel buffers and page cache are reclaimable. vmstat provides continuing observations and shows si (swap in) and so (swap out). If si and so are non-zero and frequent, your system is actively moving pages between R A M and disk. That is slow and often the primary cause of severe performance degradation. A useful workflow: run free -h to confirm current state, then vmstat 1 to watch for si/so spikes while reproducing load. A common misconception is to treat cached memory as unavailable; in fact caches are meant to be reclaimed. Concrete example: a Python process allocating a large in-memory data structure can push available memory down and trigger swap activity; vmstat will show increasing so, and response time will slow. Immediate mitigation if you cannot add R A M includes identifying and stopping nonessential memory-heavy processes or tuning application cache sizes. Remember to check swap utilization together with input and output metrics because heavy swapping will also create disk input and output pressure.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › Memory signals
Quick snapshot: free -h
              total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           16G         14G         1G         0G         1G         2G
Swap:          4G          1G         3G
Note the -/+ buffers/cache line when judging true available memory. Buffers and cache are reclaimable.
Continuous view: vmstat
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- -----cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa
 1  0  102400 1024000  51200 204800  0    256    0    128   50  100 20 10 60 10
Watch si and so for swap activity; high values indicate active swapping and poor performance.
Example
Run a memory-hungry process that allocates 1GB and observe so rising in vmstat until the allocation ends.
Common mistake
Treating cached memory as unavailable and adding unnecessary RAM when reallocating caches would suffice.
Key Takeaway

Active swap (nonzero si/so) is a reliable indicator of memory pressure and will also increase disk I/O; address the root cause rather than only adding swap space.

screens.title: Disk I/O fundamentals with iostat
screens.narratorSegment: Disk input and output bottlenecks are often subtle because they affect the whole system: C P U wait time rises and many processes appear blocked. iostat is the primary tool for diagnosing device-level issues. With iostat -x 1 you get per-device extended statistics every second. Key fields are r/s and w/s for read and write operations per second, rkB/s and wkB/s for throughput, await for average request latency, avgqu-sz for queue length, and %util for the percentage of time the device was busy. If %util is consistently near 100%, the device is saturated. High await indicates slow input and output completion times, and high avgqu-sz shows requests piling up. A combined observation of high top wa and iostat %util near 100% is a clear signal that storage is the current bottleneck. Practical steps include identifying the processes issuing the input and output and either pausing them, moving heavy input and output to off-hours, or improving storage performance. Remember, %util alone can mislead on multi-device systems; compare device-specific stats and consider queue depth and latency together. Example: running a large dd write will rapidly increase wkB/s and %util, and await will climb; monitoring these during a controlled test helps you understand device thresholds.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › iostat fundamentals
iostat - device metrics explained
Use extended stats to measure throughput, latency, and device utilization.
%util
Shows the percentage of time the device was busy. Persistent near-100% indicates saturation.
await
Average time for I/O requests. High await means requests are taking long to complete.
avgqu-sz
Average queue length. High values mean requests are waiting and the device is a bottleneck.
Concrete example — dd write
# Large sequential write to test device
dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile bs=1M count=1000 oflag=direct
# Then run: iostat -x 1 5 and watch %util, await, avgqu-sz
Key Takeaway

Match high %util with increased await and avgqu-sz to confirm a true device bottleneck before planning mitigations.

Common mistake
Relying on %util alone without checking latency measures can hide intermittent queuing and latency problems.
Pro tip
Run iostat during the suspected incident and during a controlled test to compare normal versus stressed behavior.

screens.title: Using sar for historical analysis
screens.narratorSegment: sar is different from the instant tools because it captures historical data over time. The sysstat package runs a scheduled sar collection so you can later inspect C P U, memory, and device usage for earlier periods. This is vital when a problem is intermittent and not present during an observation window. Use sar -u for C P U, sar -r for memory, and sar -b or sar -dp for input and output statistics. When you examine sar reports, look for patterns: recurring peaks at the same time of day often indicate scheduled jobs or backups; sporadic spikes may point to intermittent load from user activity or cron tasks. Example commands to inspect recent history are sar -u and sar -r; to capture new data immediately run sar in parallel and reproduce the workload. A common pitfall is not enabling sar or assuming it stores indefinitely; verify sysstat is configured to collect data and that retention settings meet your needs. Use sar reports to correlate past high %util or await values with known maintenance windows, which can save time compared with blind live troubleshooting.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › sar — historical
sar: capture and analyze historical activity
Enable sysstat collection to retain useful historical trends for later analysis.
Common commands
sar -u        # CPU usage history
sar -r        # memory history
sar -b        # I/O and transfer rates
sar -q        # run queue and load averages
Practical notes
  • Confirm sysstat cron jobs are enabled to collect sar data.
  • Look for repeating patterns to identify scheduled tasks or daily peaks.
  • Correlate sar output with logs and cron to find the root cause.
Key Takeaway

Historical data is essential for diagnosing intermittent problems that do not appear in short live observations.

Common mistake
Assuming sar is enabled by default; verify collection and retention settings on your system.
Example
Use sar to find that backups every night caused disk %util spikes and plan a staggered schedule.

screens.title: Process-level analysis: iotop, pidstat, and lsof
screens.narratorSegment: Finding the offending process is the crucial next step after establishing which resource is constrained. iotop gives a top-like view of per-process disk input and output, showing which processes generate the most reads and writes. pidstat with the -d flag reports per-process input and output statistics at intervals, which is helpful for scriptable monitoring. lsof lists open files, which can indicate which process is using a device or a large file on a particular mount. A systematic approach is: first confirm the resource type using top, vmstat, or iostat; then run iotop or pidstat to observe which PIDs drive input and output; finally use lsof to see file handles and check application logs for related activity. A common misconception is relying solely on pid or command name without confirming the role; check process context, parent processes, and whether the process is a known scheduled job. Example: when /dev/sda shows high %util, run sudo iotop to list processes with high read/write bytes and then pidstat -d 1 to confirm sustained rates. If a backup process is the culprit, coordinate schedules or throttle its input and output. Always verify PID and process name before terminating anything to avoid cascading failures.

keyIdea.title: Process attribution
keyIdea.text: Use iotop and pidstat to attribute I/O to processes and lsof to inspect open files; verify identity before taking disruptive actions.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › Process-level analysis
iotop — live I/O by process
Run with sudo to see per-process read/write bandwidth and accumulated I/O.
sudo iotop -oPa
# -o show only processes with I/O, -P accumulate, -a total
Use iotop when iostat shows device saturation to see which process is generating traffic.
pidstat & lsof
pidstat -d reports per-process I/O, lsof shows open files and device mappings.
pidstat -d 1    # per-process I/O every second
sudo lsof | grep /dev/sda  # processes with open files on device
Cross-check outputs to avoid false positives and confirm the offending process identity.
Scenario
When %util is high, use iotop to identify the writer, then check lsof and app logs to confirm purpose before stopping it.
Common mistake
Assuming the highest CPU process is the I/O offender; always verify with I/O-specific tools.
Key Takeaway

Process-level I/O tools let you pinpoint the source of device stress; verify identity before taking action to avoid collateral damage.

screens.title: Mitigation strategies and safe actions
screens.narratorSegment: Once you identify the resource and the offending process, choose an appropriate mitigation. Immediate, conservative actions include temporarily reducing process priority (renice), pausing noncritical jobs, or gracefully restarting a misbehaving service. When dealing with memory pressure, stop nonessential memory-hungry processes or reduce application cache sizes; lowering vm. swappiness can reduce swapping but may increase cache eviction and should be tested. For disk input and output issues, consider throttling backup jobs, staggering input and output loads, or using ionice to lower priority of background writers. Longer-term fixes include tuning application configurations, adding C P U cores, installing more R A M, or moving to faster storage. Always confirm the identity of the process you stop by PID and command; a common operational mistake is killing a process without checking its role, which can cascade to service failures. After applying a mitigation, monitor the same metrics you used to diagnose the issue to confirm improvement. For example, after stopping a backup job you should see iostat await and %util drop and top wa decline. Document the incident and create preventive measures such as scheduling heavy jobs outside peak hours or using capacity alerts.

narration.text: Once you identify the resource and the offending process, choose an appropriate mitigation. Immediate, conservative actions include temporarily reducing process priority (renice), pausing noncritical jobs, or gracefully restarting a misbehaving service. When dealing with memory pressure, stop nonessential memory-hungry processes or reduce application cache sizes; lowering vm. swappiness can reduce swapping but may increase cache eviction and should be tested. For disk input and output issues, consider throttling backup jobs, staggering input and output loads, or using ionice to lower priority of background writers. Longer-term fixes include tuning application configurations, adding C P U cores, installing more R A M, or moving to faster storage. Always confirm the identity of the process you stop by PID and command; a common operational mistake is killing a process without checking its role, which can cascade to service failures. After applying a mitigation, monitor the same metrics you used to diagnose the issue to confirm improvement. For example, after stopping a backup job you should see iostat await and %util drop and top wa decline. Document the incident and create preventive measures such as scheduling heavy jobs outside peak hours or using capacity alerts.

keyIdea.title: Remediation patterns
keyIdea.text: Select interventions that match the resource cause: change priorities for short-term relief, tune services for medium term, and scale hardware for long-term capacity.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › Mitigation strategies
Actions: immediate → short-term → long-term
Choose the least disruptive but effective remedy and verify with the same metrics used to diagnose the issue.
Immediate
  • Renice process or pause noncritical jobs.
  • Graceful restart of misbehaving services after verifying PID.
Short-term
  • Tune app caches, reduce connection limits, adjust vm.swappiness.
  • Throttle backup jobs with ionice or tool-specific settings.
Long-term
  • Add CPU, RAM, or faster storage where justified by capacity planning.
  • Introduce monitoring alerts tied to the metrics that reflect the bottleneck.
Key Takeaway

Mitigate safely: confirm process roles, prefer non-disruptive steps first, and monitor to confirm resolution before restorative actions.

Checklist
PID verified, logs checked, action logged, metrics rechecked.
Mistake
Killing critical daemons without a rollback plan can cause larger outages than the original problem.

screens.title: Hands-on: simulate CPU, I/O, and memory pressure
screens.narratorSegment: Reproducing load in a controlled manner is the most effective way to learn how metrics respond. For C P U load you can run yes redirected to null multiple times to consume cores, or use stress to target specific cores. For disk input and output, dd writing a large file with direct input and output quickly raises device utilization; fio provides more control for random or sequential patterns. For memory pressure, a short Python one-liner can allocate a chunk of memory until you press Enter to release it. While running these generators, watch top, vmstat, and iostat to observe expected metric shifts: C P U us rises under C P U load; iostat %util and await increase under heavy writes; vmstat si/so will show swapping when memory is exhausted. Always run generators on non-production systems or in isolated test environments and ensure you have permissions to stop the load generator. Example commands are included in the chapter activity; run them in separate terminals so you can observe both the generator and the monitoring outputs concurrently. After you reproduce and diagnose the behavior, practice applying a mitigation and confirm the metrics return toward normal. This builds confidence and reduces guesswork during real incidents.

keyIdea.title: Practice safely
keyIdea.text: Use controlled generators for CPU, I/O, and memory on test systems to learn how monitoring metrics change and to validate remediation steps.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › Hands-on simulations
CPU simulation
# multi-core stress with yes (run several times)
yes > /dev/null &
# or use stress to target cores
stress -c 1 &
Observe top and watch us increase and the run queue grow under sustained CPU load.
Disk I/O simulation
# large sequential write
dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile bs=1M count=1000 oflag=direct &
# or use fio for more patterns
fio --name=randwrite --ioengine=posixaio --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --size=1G --numjobs=1 --iodepth=1 --filename=/tmp/fio_test.tmp &
Run iostat -x 1 to watch %util and await increase while the write runs.
Memory simulation
# allocate ~1GB and wait for Enter to free it
python3 -c "a = ' ' * (1024**3); input('Press Enter to free memory')" &
Key Takeaway

Always run generators in isolated test environments and monitor metrics concurrently to validate signatures before applying fixes in production.

Safety
Do not run heavy generators on production without maintenance windows and clear rollback plans.
Verify
After mitigation, re-run the same monitoring to confirm metrics return to expected ranges.

screens.title: Interpreting combined signals
screens.narratorSegment: Solving real incidents requires correlating outputs from multiple tools rather than relying on a single indicator. For example, top may show high C P U usage, but if wa is also high and iostat shows %util near 100%, disk input and output is likely the root cause. Conversely, if top shows high us and iostat shows low %util and low await, the problem is C P U-bound. For memory issues, vmstat showing frequent si/so alongside heavy iostat traffic indicates swapping is contributing to disk load. A practical interpretation workflow is: capture top and note wa/us/sy, start iostat -x 1 to check device %util and await, and run vmstat 1 to see si/so. If multiple signals point to the same resource, you can be confident in your diagnosis; if signals are mixed, prioritize the one with the clearest resource-specific counters (e. g., %util and await for disks). A common error is acting on a single tool snapshot taken during a transient spike. Always gather short time-series from the tools while reproducing or observing the incident before taking disruptive action. That reduces the chance of misdiagnosis and ensures your remediation addresses the actual bottleneck.

keyIdea.title: Correlation
keyIdea.text: Use combined, time-aligned outputs from top, vmstat, and iostat to confidently identify the true bottleneck and avoid incorrect fixes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › Correlating signals
Correlate metrics to avoid misdiagnosis
Collect aligned time-series from multiple tools while the issue is active.
Symptom set: high wa
top shows high wa; check iostat %util and await. If %util ≈ 100% and await is high, storage is the bottleneck.
Symptom set: high si/so
vmstat shows heavy swap; look for increased disk I/O as a side effect and identify memory-hungry processes.
Symptom set: high us
Top shows high user CPU while iostat remains quiet; consider CPU-bound code, parallelism, or inefficient algorithms.
Key Takeaway

Align short time-series from top, iostat, and vmstat to form a consistent diagnosis before taking corrective action.

Action
Capture outputs for 30–60 seconds while reproducing the issue if possible; store logs for postmortem analysis.
Mistake
Relying on a single instantaneous reading often leads to the wrong root cause and ineffective remediation.

screens.title: Swap management and vm.swappiness
screens.narratorSegment: Swap is disk space used as virtual memory when physical R A M is exhausted. While swap prevents immediate out-of-memory kills, accessing swapped pages is orders of magnitude slower than R A M and causes system-wide slowdowns. The kernel parameter vm. swappiness controls how aggressively the kernel moves anonymous pages to swap. A higher swappiness causes earlier swapping, while a lower value keeps pages in R A M longer and relies on page cache reclamation first. In practice, many systems work well with a moderately low swappiness value, but changing it is a trade-off: reducing swappiness can reduce swap usage and improve interactivity, but it may increase cache pressure. When diagnosing swap-related performance issues, rely on vmstat si/so values and free -h to confirm active swap usage; then consider killing or tuning memory-hungry applications before adjusting swappiness. Example immediate actions include identifying the culprit process and terminating it if safe, or reducing application memory footprints. Remember: adjusting swappiness is a band-aid for workload memory demand; appropriate long-term solutions include adding R A M or reconfiguring applications to use less memory.

keyIdea.title: Swap guidance
keyIdea.text: Swap prevents crashes but hurts performance; adjust swappiness carefully and prioritize reducing memory demand or adding RAM for lasting fixes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.5 › Swap & swappiness
Swap behavior and tuning
Understand why swapping drastically reduces performance and how vm.swappiness influences kernel choices.
What swap does
Provides virtual memory on disk to avoid immediate process termination when RAM is exhausted.
Why it's slow
Accessing swapped pages requires disk operations, which are vastly slower than RAM and can increase I/O wait.
Tuning
Adjust vm.swappiness via sysctl to influence when the kernel swaps, but treat it as a temporary mitigation.
Key Takeaway

Reduce memory demand or add RAM for sustained performance; changing swappiness can help temporarily but does not replace capacity planning.

Example action
sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10 to test a lower swappiness value; monitor si/so and application behavior.
Mistake
Using swappiness as a substitute for fixing memory leaks or right-sizing application memory settings.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should retain. First, identify the resource type from its metric signature: C P U-bound work shows high user or system C P U, memory pressure shows active swapping with si/so, and disk input and output bottlenecks show high iostat %util with high await and increased top wa. Second, use the right tool: top and htop for live process and C P U views, vmstat and free for memory and swap visibility, iostat for device-level input and output and latency, and sar for historical trend analysis. Third, attribute the load to a process using iotop, pidstat, and lsof before taking disruptive actions. Fourth, choose remediation that matches the cause: renice or stop processes for immediate relief, tune applications or schedules for medium-term fixes, and add resources for long-term capacity. Practice these steps in a safe test environment and always re-measure to confirm improvements. These concepts form a systematic workflow from symptom to root cause and solution.

Each exhausted resource has characteristic metrics you must learn to read.

top / htop

fullNarratorScript:
Resource exhaustion is a leading cause of slow servers, intermittent failures, and unpredictable behavior. In this lesson you will learn how to recognize the symptoms of C P U, memory, and disk input and output pressure, how to collect both real-time and historical evidence, and how to identify the process or configuration that needs attention. We will use standard Linux tools — top and htop for live process views, vmstat and free for memory and swap signals, iostat for device latency and utilization, and sar for historical trends. You will also see how to tie signals together: for example, high C P U wait time often reflects a disk bottleneck, while sustained swapping points to memory exhaustion. The practical demos show simple generators to reproduce pressure safely, which helps you practice interpreting metrics. By the end you will be able to locate the offending process, choose immediate mitigation steps, and plan longer-term fixes such as tuning, capacity changes, or configuration updates. Think of this chapter as a toolkit for turning vague slowness into a targeted action plan.

Over the next screens you'll develop measurable skills for diagnosing resource exhaustion. First, you'll learn to recognize the symptoms of C P U, memory, and disk input and output saturation and to distinguish which resource is the root cause. Second, you'll gain hands-on familiarity with real-time tools such as top, htop, vmstat, and iostat so you can collect the right metrics quickly during incidents. Third, you will practice process-level analysis: identifying which process generates the load, using tools that report per-process C P U, memory, and input and output. Finally, you'll learn mitigation patterns: immediate actions like safely stopping a runaway process, short-term kernel or configuration tweaks, and longer-term fixes like tuning application settings or adding capacity. Each objective combines a practical command set with the reasoning that explains why a metric indicates a specific bottleneck. A verified competency milestone follows every card so you can self-check that you can both run the commands and interpret the results correctly.

These next objectives expand the core skills with tool-specific interpretations and historical analysis. First, you will learn to interpret key fields: in top, understand the meaning of us, sy and wa; in iostat, learn what %util and await reveal about device latency. Second, you will gain practical experience with swap and vm. swappiness so you understand why active swapping hurts performance and how to reduce swap pressure safely. Third, you'll become comfortable using sar for historical analysis to spot intermittent peaks and recurring load patterns. Finally, you'll practice safe simulation and testing: generating controlled C P U, input and output, and memory load and then using the monitoring toolset to confirm the expected metric changes. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can demonstrate both execution of the commands and correct interpretation of results in a debugging scenario.

Resource exhaustion means one of the system's primary resources — C P U, memory, or disk input and output — is saturated and cannot meet demand. Symptoms often include sluggish interactive response, long application latencies, or processes stalling and crashing. The critical teaching point is that different resources create different signatures: C P U exhaustion increases user or system C P U percentages, but disk input and output problems frequently show up as high C P U wait time, meaning the C P U is idle while waiting for input and output. Memory exhaustion leads to heavy swapping, where pages are moved to disk and performance collapses. Correct identification matters because the remediation differs: killing a C P U-bound process frees C P U cycles, but killing a process that is causing heavy disk input and output might not immediately reduce wait time if the device remains saturated. A practical misconception to avoid is treating a high overall C P U usage number as a single cause; you must inspect detailed counters such as wa, si, and so. A quick example: if interactive shell prompts lag while top shows high wa and iostat shows %util near 100%, adding C P U cores will not fix the problem — faster storage or reducing input and output load will. Takeaway: look for the signature, not just the headline metric.

top and htop are your first-stop tools when a system feels slow. top gives a compact summary: load averages, C P U states, memory use, and a process list. Important fields to interpret include us (user C P U), sy (system C P U), and wa (input and output wait). High us suggests compute-bound processes, high sy points to kernel activity, and high wa indicates the C P U is waiting on input and output. htop offers the same data in a more readable, colorized form and simplifies actions such as sorting by memory or C P U and sending signals to processes. A common workflow: sort by C P U and note the top consumers, then switch sorting by memory to find processes holding large resident sets. Watch the run queue length too — a growing runnable queue combined with high us suggests adding C P U capacity or tuning parallelism. A typical mistake is focusing solely on the top process without checking overall C P U wait and device metrics. For example, if a process shows high C P U but wa is also high, some of the apparent C P U time may be caused by blocking input and output or kernel work. Practice: run top while inducing a C P U load generator and observe how us rises sharply; then induce disk input and output and see wa increase while the top process may still appear active. This practice helps you translate numbers into root causes.

Memory exhaustion shows up as low available memory and active swapping. The free command with human-readable flags gives a quick snapshot of total and available memory, as well as swap size and use. Pay attention to the line labeled -/+ buffers/cache which better reflects memory available to applications because kernel buffers and page cache are reclaimable. vmstat provides continuing observations and shows si (swap in) and so (swap out). If si and so are non-zero and frequent, your system is actively moving pages between R A M and disk. That is slow and often the primary cause of severe performance degradation. A useful workflow: run free -h to confirm current state, then vmstat 1 to watch for si/so spikes while reproducing load. A common misconception is to treat cached memory as unavailable; in fact caches are meant to be reclaimed. Concrete example: a Python process allocating a large in-memory data structure can push available memory down and trigger swap activity; vmstat will show increasing so, and response time will slow. Immediate mitigation if you cannot add R A M includes identifying and stopping nonessential memory-heavy processes or tuning application cache sizes. Remember to check swap utilization together with input and output metrics because heavy swapping will also create disk input and output pressure.

Disk input and output bottlenecks are often subtle because they affect the whole system: C P U wait time rises and many processes appear blocked. iostat is the primary tool for diagnosing device-level issues. With iostat -x 1 you get per-device extended statistics every second. Key fields are r/s and w/s for read and write operations per second, rkB/s and wkB/s for throughput, await for average request latency, avgqu-sz for queue length, and %util for the percentage of time the device was busy. If %util is consistently near 100%, the device is saturated. High await indicates slow input and output completion times, and high avgqu-sz shows requests piling up. A combined observation of high top wa and iostat %util near 100% is a clear signal that storage is the current bottleneck. Practical steps include identifying the processes issuing the input and output and either pausing them, moving heavy input and output to off-hours, or improving storage performance. Remember, %util alone can mislead on multi-device systems; compare device-specific stats and consider queue depth and latency together. Example: running a large dd write will rapidly increase wkB/s and %util, and await will climb; monitoring these during a controlled test helps you understand device thresholds.

sar is different from the instant tools because it captures historical data over time. The sysstat package runs a scheduled sar collection so you can later inspect C P U, memory, and device usage for earlier periods. This is vital when a problem is intermittent and not present during an observation window. Use sar -u for C P U, sar -r for memory, and sar -b or sar -dp for input and output statistics. When you examine sar reports, look for patterns: recurring peaks at the same time of day often indicate scheduled jobs or backups; sporadic spikes may point to intermittent load from user activity or cron tasks. Example commands to inspect recent history are sar -u and sar -r; to capture new data immediately run sar in parallel and reproduce the workload. A common pitfall is not enabling sar or assuming it stores indefinitely; verify sysstat is configured to collect data and that retention settings meet your needs. Use sar reports to correlate past high %util or await values with known maintenance windows, which can save time compared with blind live troubleshooting.

Finding the offending process is the crucial next step after establishing which resource is constrained. iotop gives a top-like view of per-process disk input and output, showing which processes generate the most reads and writes. pidstat with the -d flag reports per-process input and output statistics at intervals, which is helpful for scriptable monitoring. lsof lists open files, which can indicate which process is using a device or a large file on a particular mount. A systematic approach is: first confirm the resource type using top, vmstat, or iostat; then run iotop or pidstat to observe which PIDs drive input and output; finally use lsof to see file handles and check application logs for related activity. A common misconception is relying solely on pid or command name without confirming the role; check process context, parent processes, and whether the process is a known scheduled job. Example: when /dev/sda shows high %util, run sudo iotop to list processes with high read/write bytes and then pidstat -d 1 to confirm sustained rates. If a backup process is the culprit, coordinate schedules or throttle its input and output. Always verify PID and process name before terminating anything to avoid cascading failures.
